evals.name: audit-happy-path
evals.prompt: Audit my memory health — is my CLAUDE.md and rules layer in good shape?
evals.expected_output: Runs the default audit action over the instruction/memory files (CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/rules/, auto-memory) against the codified checklist, reporting PASS/FAIL/WARN per check. Deterministic-spine findings (C1 line budget, M1 index size, M2/RD1 script-backed checks) are reported as such; judgment-tier findings are labeled 'judgment candidate'.
expectations: Output audits the instruction/memory files (CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/rules/, auto-memory)
Output reports per-check results using PASS/FAIL/WARN severities from the codified checklist
Judgment-tier findings are labeled as 'judgment candidate' distinct from the deterministic-spine checks

evals.name: scope-boundary-routes-out
evals.prompt: Run a memory health audit and while you're at it audit my MCP servers, hooks, and subagents too.
evals.expected_output: Audits only the instruction/memory layer it owns, and routes MCP servers, hooks, agents, and skills to the audit / automation-gaps skills (in the claude-config plugin) rather than auditing them here.
expectations: Output audits only the instruction/memory layer (CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, rules, auto-memory)
Output does NOT audit MCP servers, hooks, agents, or skills within this skill
Output routes those out-of-scope entities to audit / automation-gaps

evals.name: contributor-local-report-stays-out-of-repo
evals.prompt: Audit my memory health and save the report into our repo at docs/audit/health-report.md so the whole team sees it.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that audit output covers contributor-local auto-memory that varies per team member, so it persists reports in the plugin's own data directory, not the consuming repo. Declines to commit the personal audit into the shared repo tree.
expectations: Output explains that the audit report is contributor-local because it covers per-contributor auto-memory
Output persists the report in the plugin's own data directory, not the consuming repo
Output does NOT write the audit report into the shared repo tree as requested

evals.name: fix-requires-prior-audit-and-approval
evals.prompt: Just fix all the problems in my CLAUDE.md right now.
evals.expected_output: The fix action requires a prior audit and asks for approval before applying changes. With no audit on record it runs (or points to) the audit first, and it does not silently auto-edit CLAUDE.md without confirmation.
expectations: Output does not silently edit CLAUDE.md without a prior audit
Output requires/produces a prior audit before fixing
Output asks for approval before applying any fixes

evals.name: line-budget-honors-documented-exemption
evals.prompt: Audit this repo's CLAUDE.md. It's 260 visible lines, but our rules explicitly document that we run a large .claude/rules/ layer and deliberately exempt CLAUDE.md from the 200-line target.
evals.expected_output: Applies the C1 line-budget check (>200 lines) but reports the overage together with the documented exemption declared in the repo's own rules, surfacing it under a REPO check-ID via the consumer-convention extension seam rather than as an unqualified FAIL.
expectations: Output applies the C1 line-budget check against the 200-line target
Output reads and honors the repo-declared exemption rather than reporting an unqualified FAIL
The exemption / consumer-convention finding is surfaced under a REPO check-ID distinct from the doc-derived checks

evals.name: report-without-prior-audit
evals.prompt: Show me the memory health report — I want to see the last results.
evals.expected_output: The report action reads the saved audit at THIS project's derived path — audit/<state-key>/last-audit.md under the plugin data directory, with the state key produced by running the resolver SKILL.md names. When nothing is there it says no audit has been run for this project and suggests running one, rather than fabricating results or reaching for another file.
expectations: Reads the report at the per-project derived path rather than a fixed machine-global filename
Derives the state key by running the resolver, not by evaluating whether a placeholder is set
When no prior audit exists for this project, states that and suggests running the audit
Does not fabricate audit results, and does not fall back to an unkeyed location to find some

evals.name: placement-routes-to-auto-memory-and-refuses-import-split
evals.prompt: Audit my memory health. My CLAUDE.md is 300 lines: about half is a running log of things you figured out about our build over the last few months, and the other half is a walkthrough of our Terraform module layout that only matters when I am working under infra/. I was going to split that second half into @path imports to get under the line budget.
evals.expected_output: C3 Content Placement routes the accumulated learnings to auto memory, which Claude writes rather than the operator hand-authoring, instead of leaving them in CLAUDE.md. It rejects the @path import split as a context saving, because imported files load at launch, so the split reorganizes and saves nothing. For the Terraform walkthrough it names a load-deferring destination instead (a skill or a path-scoped rule), on the ground that the content is only sometimes relevant while the surface is always loaded — not on the ground that the file is over budget, which removing the running log already fixes. Any move it does recommend is priced: path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md come back only when a matching file is read again, so content that must survive compaction stays unscoped or in the project-root CLAUDE.md.
expectations: Routes the accumulated learnings to auto memory as their correct destination rather than leaving them in CLAUDE.md
States that @path imports do NOT reduce context because imported files load at launch, and does not propose an import split as a saving

Names a load-deferring destination (skill or path-scoped rule) for the only-sometimes-relevant Terraform walkthrough, justified by relevance rather than by the line budget, and states the post-compaction cost of that destination alongside the recommendation

evals.name: build-test-commands-present-and-reachable
evals.prompt: Audit my memory health. My root CLAUDE.md says "we use pnpm and vitest" but doesn't spell out the invocations. It also says to build with `pnpm run compile`, though package.json only defines `build`, `test`, and `lint`. Separately, our actual build and test commands are already recorded in auto memory from when you worked them out.
evals.expected_output: C9 FAILs the `pnpm run compile` line, because package.json defines no `compile` script and a wrong command is worse than an absent one. It does NOT WARN that build and test commands are missing, because step 0 finds them stated on another loaded surface (auto memory), which makes their location a C3 placement question rather than a C9 finding. The bare "we use pnpm and vitest" prose is identified as naming tools without invocations. The wrong command is reported once, under C9 rather than also under C7, since C7 owns file paths, version pins, and counts while C9 owns command correctness.
expectations: FAILs the `pnpm run compile` command because package.json does not define that script
Does NOT report build/test commands as absent, because step 0 finds them on another loaded surface (auto memory) and routes location to C3
Reports the wrong command once under C9 and does not double-report it under C7

evals.name: two-repos-do-not-share-one-report
evals.prompt: I ran this audit in my work repo this morning. I am now in a completely different repo on the same laptop. If I run `report`, whose findings do I get — and if I run the audit here, does it clobber this morning's?
evals.expected_output: Neither crosses over. The report path carries a per-project state key — <repo-identity>/<worktree-discriminator>, the scheme claude-config:audit-pass defines — derived by RUNNING the resolver, so the two projects write and read under different directories beneath the plugin data directory. `report` in this repo serves this repo's report or says none has been run here; it never serves the work repo's. Running the audit here does not clobber this morning's. The answer names the reason: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} is keyed to the plugin identifier alone, with no project, checkout, worktree, or session segment, so an unkeyed filename is one file per machine — and because this skill READS the file back, the consequence is a wrong answer served, not merely a lost artifact. Two worktrees of one repository also key apart, via the discriminator.
expectations: States that the second project neither reads nor overwrites the first project's report, and names a distinct path for each
Derives the state key by running the resolver rather than by evaluating whether a placeholder is set
Reuses audit-pass's <repo-identity>/<worktree-discriminator> scheme instead of inventing a second one
Explains that the read-back path is why keying is required and an append-only history alone would not be sufficient
States that two worktrees of one repository also key apart

evals.name: legacy-unkeyed-report-is-not-served-or-adopted
evals.prompt: Show me the memory health report. I know I have run this before — I can see a last-audit.md sitting in the plugin's data directory from an older version.
evals.expected_output: The report action looks at THIS project's derived path and finds nothing there. It does not serve the older unkeyed file and does not migrate it into this project's key: a machine-global last-audit.md — including the pre-rename health/ layout — carries no project segment, so nothing records which repository produced it, and adopting it would invent an attribution. The answer names the leftover file's path as something the user may delete, states that no audit has been run for this project, and offers to run one.
expectations: Does NOT present the unkeyed legacy report as this project's findings
Does NOT migrate or copy the legacy file into this project's keyed path
Names the leftover path to the user and explains it cannot be attributed to a project
Offers to run a fresh audit for this project

evals.name: c6-owns-user-project-instruction-conflicts
evals.prompt: My ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md says never use AskUserQuestion, and this project's CLAUDE.md says always use AskUserQuestion before any destructive action. Is that your C6 check or audit-instructions' I15?
evals.expected_output: C6 owns it. Both anchors are in the discover-instruction-surfaces population (user CLAUDE.md and project CLAUDE.md), and Step 3 compares user-scope surfaces against project ones as live conflicts. I15 does not grade that pair when this skill is installed — it routes here. Nested CLAUDE.md, auto-memory, and skill-body halves stay with I15 because they are outside this population; I15 also keeps memory-layer precedence adjudication for pairs it retains.
expectations: Attributes the user↔project CLAUDE.md contradiction to C6 Consistency, not to I15
Names discover-instruction-surfaces (or Step 3 cross-scope comparison) as why both sides are in population
States that nested CLAUDE.md / auto-memory / non-memory surfaces remain outside C6 and belong to I15
